application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

abstract.div:
Bonifaci et al. have recently [5]
introduced some novel analytical techniques in order to derive a speed-up bound for the multiprocessor global EDF scheduling of systems of recurrent tasks that are represented using the sporadic DAG task model, and have applied these techniques to obtain a pseudopolynomial time sufficient schedulability test. In this paper, these techniques are further generalized to yield an improved pseudopolynomial time sufficient schedulability test for global EDF scheduling of systems of sporadic DAG tasks. It is shown that this new test strictly dominates the one in [5]; in addition, schedulability experiments demonstrate that the improvement can be quite substantial for certain kinds of task systems.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: Multiprocessor real-time scheduling theory started out considering the scheduling of recurrent task systems that are represented using relatively simple task models such as Liu & Layland [8] or 3-parameter sporadic [6], [9] tasks. One important characteristic of these early models is that the work generated by each individual recurrent task is assumed to be completely sequential: any particular task is allowed to execute upon at most one processor at each instant in time. This research has, by and large, been very successful; encouraged by the success in these initial endeavors, more expressive models, that are able to represent the parallelism that may be present within each individual recurrent task, are beginning to be considered. One particularly powerful such model in the sporadic DAG model for recurrent real-time tasks [3].

In the sporadic DAG model, a task τ i is specified as a 3-tuple (G i , D i , T i ), where G i is a directed acyclic graph (DAG), and D i and T i are positive integers. The task τ i repeatedly releases dag-jobs, each of which is a collection of (sequential) jobs. Successive dag-jobs are released a duration of at least T i time units apart. The DAG G i is specified as G i = (V i , E i ), where V i is a set of vertices and E i a set of directed edges between these vertices. Each v ∈ V i denotes a sequential operation (a "job"), and is characterized by a worst-case execution time (WCET). The edges represent dependencies between the jobs: if (v 1 , v 2 ) ∈ E i then job v 1 must complete execution before job v 2 can begin execution. (Job v 1 is then called a predecessor job of v 2 .) A release of a dag-job of τ i at time-instant t means that all |V i | jobs v ∈ V i are released at time-instant t. As stated above, the period T i denotes the minimum duration of time that must elapse between the release of successive dag-jobs of τ i . If a dag-job is released at time-instant t then all |V i | jobs that were released at t must complete execution by time-instant t + D i . Some recent work [5], [7] has greatly enhanced our understanding of the multiprocessor global-EDF (GEDF) scheduling of collections of such sporadic DAG tasks. Two papers [5], [7] presented at ECRTS last year independently showed that GEDF has a speedup bound of (2 -1/m) when implemented upon an m-processor platform. In addition to proving this speedup bound, [5] derives a pseudo-polynomial time GEDFschedulability test with speedup bound of (2 -1/m + ) for any constant > 0. (To our knowledge, [7] does not have an effective schedulability test that ensures similar speedup bounds.) This work. These results in [5], [7] are immensely important and interesting from a theoretical perspective since they show that GEDF is optimal to within a speedup factor of 2. Further, the results in [5] actually yield an effective polynomialtime schedulability test such that any system passing this test is guaranteed to be successfully scheduled using GEDF. However, we will show in this paper that the schedulability test derived in [5] does not fully exploit all the insight gained in its proof of the speedup bound. Informally speaking -this is discussed more thoroughly in Section III -the schedulability test presented in [5] seeks to establish GEDFschedulability of a given system by identifying a "witness" to such schedulability, where a potential witness is any real number between 0 and 1 possessing some desired properties (specified in Definition 1). The GEDF-schedulability test in [5] checks only whether a single number (m/(2m -1), where m is the number of processors) is a witness, and reports failure if this turns out to not be a witness. In this paper we derive an algorithm to optimally discover a witness if one exists. Hence our test correctly identifies all systems that can be shown to be GEDF-schedulable on the basis of the insights of [5], and therefore dominates the test of [5].

Organization. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. In Section II we formally define the sporadic DAG tasks model, and introduce some notation and terminology that will be used in the remainder of this paper. In Section III we provide a brief overview of the techniques introduced in [5] that we seek to extend in this paper. In Section IV we derive our new and improved GEDF-schedulability test for sporadic DAG task systems; additionally, we prove (i) its correctness, and (ii) its dominance over the earlier test in [5]. We have conducted schedulability experiments on randomly-generated task systems to further demonstrate the superiority of our schedulabiltiy test over previously-proposed ones; we report our findings of these experiments in Section V. We conclude in Section VI by placing this work within the larger context of the GEDF schedulability analysis of recurrent task systems upon identical multiprocessor platforms.

div.head: II. MODEL AND DEFINITIONS
div.p: We seek to schedule a given collection of n sporadic DAG tasks τ 1 , τ 2 , . . . , τ n upon m unit-speed processors. Each task
div.formula: τ i is specified by a tuple (G i , D i , T i ), where G i = (V i , E i )
div.p: is a vertex-weighted directed acyclic graph, and D i and T i are positive integers. In this paper, we restrict our attention to constrained deadline systems: those in which D i ≤ T i for all tasks τ i in the system.
An example sporadic DAG task is depicted graphically in Figure 1. Some additional notation and terminology:
div.formula: • A chain in DAG task τ i is a sequence of vertices v 1 , v 2 , . . . , v k ∈ V i such that (v j , v j+1 ) is an edge in G i , 1 ≤ j < k.
div.p: The length of this chain is defined to be the sum of the WCETs of all the vertices in the chain:

k j=1 e vj . We denote by len i the length of the longest chain in the DAG G i . For our example DAG task τ 1 of Figure 1, len 1 = 6. • We denote by vol i = v∈Vi e v the total WCET of each dag-job of τ i . For our example DAG task τ 1 of Figure 1, vol 1 = 9. • For each task τ i we define a density δ i = len i /D i and a utilization U i = vol i /T i . For our example DAG task τ 1 of Figure 1, δ 1 = 6/16 = 0.375, while U 1 = 9/20 = 0.45. • For a DAG sporadic task system τ we define its maximum density δ max (τ ) to be the largest density of any task in τ : δ max (τ ) = max τi∈τ {δ i }; its utilization U (τ ) to be the sum of the utilizations of all the tasks in τ : U (τ ) = τi∈τ U i ; and its hyperperiod P (τ ) to be the least common multiple of the period parameters of all the tasks in τ :
div.formula: P (τ ) = lcm τi∈τ {T i }.
div.p: Parallelism in the DAG. The sporadic DAG task model generalizes sequential recurrent task models such as the Liu and

Layland model [8] or the 3-parameter model [9] in the sense that each task may generate work that can be simultaneously executed upon more than one processor. We characterize the parallelism of a DAG task in the following manner. Suppose that we had an unbounded number of unit-speed processors available, and consider the schedule of a dag-job of τ i upon these processors. Let λ i,0 = 0, λ i,1 , . . . , λ i,ki = len i denote the instants at which the number of processors used changesthis reflects a change in the degree of parallelism of the dagjob. It is evident that k i is no larger than the number of vertices |V i | in the DAG. For 0 ≤ j < k i , let ν i,j denote the number of processors used (and hence, the degree of parallelism) over the duration [λ i,j , λ i,j+1 ]. For notational convenience, let ν i,ki = 0.
Example 1. Figure 2 illustrates the parallelism within each dag-job of the example sporadic DAG task τ 1 of Figure 1.
Fig. 2: The parallelism within each dag-job of the task τ1 of Figure 1.

The DAG has two source nodes (i.e., nodes with no predecessors); these may both execute immediately the dag-job is released. Therefore, ν 1,0 = 2. One of these completes upon having executed for one unit (thus, λ 1,1 = 1); however, its successor node can only begin executing when both source nodes have completed execution. When this happens, this single job executes for a further two units of execution. We therefore have λ 1,2 = 4 and ν 1,1 = 1. Upon the completion of this job, its three successor jobs may each begin execution. Two of these successor jobs complete upon having executed for one unit; the remaining job executes for an additional unit. This is reflected by having λ 1,3 = 5 with ν 1,2 = 3, and λ 1,4 = 6 with ν 1,3 = 1.

The notation introduced in this section for describing sporadic DAG task systems is summarized in Figure 3. III. A REVIEW OF THE METHODOLOGY OF [5] Bonifaci et al. [5] introduced the notion of a work function to characterize the amount of work that could be generated by a sporadic DAG task. We now describe their work function in a manner consistent with the terminology introduced in Section II.

Let τ i denote a sporadic DAG task, and s any positive real number ≤ 1. Let J denote any collection of jobs legally generated by the task τ i .
• For an interval I, let work(J, I, s) denote the amount of execution occurring within the interval I in the schedule S ∞ (J, s), of jobs with deadlines that fall within I.

Observe that since schedule S ∞ (J, s) executes each job as soon as it becomes available, thereby leaving as little work to be done later as possible, every schedule for J on speed-s processors meeting all deadlines has to complete at least work(J, I, s) units of execution over the interval I. • For any positive integer t, let work(J, t, s) denote the maximum value work(J, I, s) can take, over any interval I of duration equal to t. • Finally, let work(τ i , t, s) denote the maximum value of work(J, t, s), over all job sequences J that may be generated by the sporadic DAG task τ i .

Let us further extend the definition of the work function from individual tasks to task systems in an obvious manner: for any DAG task system τ , let work(τ, t, s) denote the sum τi∈τ work(τ i , t, s). Claim 1 below immediately follows from the definitions of maximum density and the work function:

Claim 1. Far a sporadic DAG task system τ to be feasible (always schedulable to meet all deadlines by an optimal, clairvoyant scheduler) upon m speed-s processors, it is necessary that 1) δ max (τ ) ≤ s, and 2) ∀t : t ≥ 0 : work(τ, t, s) ≤ ms.
The main result of [5] may be stated as follows.
Theorem 1
div.formula: ([5]). Let α denote any constant ≥ 1. Sporadic DAG task system τ is GEDF schedulable on m speed-α processors if δ max (τ ) ≤ 1,and
work(τ, t, 1) ≤ (αm -(m -1)) × t
div.p: for all values of t ≥ 0.

In performing schdulability analysis, we typically assume that we have unit-speed processors available to us, and seek to determine whether a system is guaranteed to be scheduled such that all jobs of all tasks will always complete by their deadlines. While Theorem 1 was very useful in [5] for establishing that the speedup bound for the global EDF is (2 -1/m), it is not immediately obvious how it can be used to determine whether a given sporadic DAG task system is global EDF schedulable or not upon unit-speed processors. We now restate the result of Theorem 1 in a manner that allows us to answer this question. Let σ denote any constant < 1. It is possible to mimic the derivation of Theorem 1 in [5], with "unit-speed" replaced by σ and α replaced by 1, to get Theorem 2. Let σ denote any constant < 1. Sporadic DAG task system τ is global-EDF schedulable on m unit-speed processors if δ max (τ ) ≤ σ, and
div.formula: work(τ, t, σ) ≤ (m -(m -1)σ) × t (1)
div.p: for all values of t ≥ 0.

Hence to show that a given τ is EDF-schedulable upon m unit-speed processors it suffices, according to Theorem 2 above, to produce a value for σ such that Condition 1 holds for all t ≥ 0. Let us refer to such a σ as a witness to the EDF-schedulability of τ .

div.head: Definition 1 (witness). Any positive real number σ for which
div.p: Condition 1 holds for all t ≥ 0 is a witness to the EDF schedulability of sporadic DAG task system τ upon m unitspeed processors.

Limitation of the GEDF-schedulability test in [5]. The schedulability test presented in [5] essentially reduces to determining whether σ ← m/(2m -1) is a witness to the EDF-schedulability of τ . It turns out that this is sufficient for establishing the speedup bound of (2 -1/m), which was the main purpose of the derivation in [5]. However, by testing only one out of all the values of σ that could potentially be a witness to a task system's schedulability, the test in [5] clearly fails to make full use of the insight into EDF-schedulability that the results in [5] afford us. In Section IV below, we derive an algorithm that fully exploits the insights of [5], by correctly identifying all task systems for which any σ would cause Inequality 1 to evaluate to true for all t ≥ 0. In other words, the algorithm in Section IV identifies all systems satisfying Theorem 2, whereas the test in [5] only identifies those systems that satisfy this condition instantiated with σ ← m/(2m -1).

div.head: A. Computing the work function
div.p: Above we have defined work(τ i , t, s) to be the maximum value of work(J, t, s), over all job sequences J that may be generated by the sporadic DAG task τ i . It is evident that this maximum is achieved when the deadline of some dag-job of τ i coincides with the rightmost endpoint of an interval of duration t, and the other dag-jobs of τ i are released as closely as possible. This is illustrated in Example 3 below.

div.head: IV. A SCHEDULABILITY TEST
div.p: In order to show that a given τ is EDF-schedulable upon m unit-speed processors it suffices, according to Theorem 2 above, to produce a witness to this fact: a value for σ such that Condition 1 holds for all t ≥ 0. As we had stated earlier, the schedulability test presented in [5] essentially reduces to determining whether σ ← m/(2m -1) is a witness to the EDF-schedulability of τ . In the remainder of this section, we derive an algorithm that correctly identifies all task systems for which any σ would cause Inequality 1 to evaluate to true for all t ≥ 0. In this manner, the algorithm derived here fully exploits the insights of [5] by identifying as GEDF-schedulable all task systems whose schedulability is implied by Theorem 2 -in contrast to the test in [5], which only identifies those systems for which m/(2m -1) is a witness to their GEDFschedulability.

Given a DAG sporadic task system τ and m unit-speed processors, we construct a solution to the problem of determining whether there is a witness to the GEDF-schedulability of τ upon these m processors by answering the following two questions.

1) In order to determine whether a particular σ is indeed a witness to the GEDF-schedulability or not, for which values of t do we actually need to evaluate Condition 1? (observe that Condition 1 is universally quantified over all time durations t, i.e., it must be shown to hold for all t); and

2) Which values of σ would we need to consider as potential witnesses to the EDF-schedulability of τ ? This overall approach is inspired by, and therefore very similar to, the ones presented in [1], [2] in the context of deriving an improved schedulability test for 3-parameter sporadic [6], [9] task systems.

div.head: A. Bounding the range of time values to be tested
div.p: We turn our attention to the first of the questions listed above. Informally speaking, Claim 2 below asserts that we only need to evaluate Condition 1 at those values of t at which the slope of the work function work i (τ i , t, σ) changes for some τ i ∈ τ .

Therefore, the LHS of Condition 1 increases with constant slope with increasing t between two consecutive t's in the set of values represented by Expression 2 above. Since the RHS of Condition 1 also increases with constant slope with increasing t, it is guaranteed that if this condition is violated at some t it will be violated at one of the two t's in this set that neighbor t.

div.head: B. Choosing potential witnesses to test
div.p: We now turn our attention to the second of the two questions listed earlier in this section, and ask: Which values of σ would we need to consider as potential witnesses to the EDFschedulability of τ ? Claim 5. No value of σ that is greater than m -U (τ ) m -1 can possibly result in Condition 1 evaluating to true for all values of t (and hence, no such value of σ can attest to the EDF-schedulability of τ ).

Proof: Observe that work(τ i , t, σ) asymptotically approaches t × (vol i /T i ) as t → ∞. Hence work(τ, t, σ) asymptotically approaches t×U (τ ) with increasing t. In order to have work(τ, t, σ) ≤ (m -(m -1)σ)t for all t, therefore, we need
div.formula: U (τ ) ≤ m -(m -1)σ ⇔ σ ≤ m -U (τ ) m -1
div.p: As a consequence of Claim 5 above, we can restrict the range of values for σ that are potential witnesses to the EDF-schedulability of τ . However, there are still infinitely many distinct values in this range, and we clearly cannot exhaustively check all these infinitely many values. Fortunately it so happens that we can restrict the actual number of values of σ within this range that need be considered as potential witnesses to the EDF-schedulability of τ , as we will now show.

div.head: C. Putting the pieces together: the EDF schedulability test
div.p: We are now ready to put the pieces together, and specify our schedulability test. This schedulability test is a systematic quest for a witness to the EDF-schedulability of τ ; i.e., for a value of σ for which there is no t causing Condition 1 to evaluate to false. Based on Claim 6, we will start out testing a small value for σ; if this value of σ turns out to not be a witness to the EDF-schedulability of τ , we can try a larger value for σ and use the result of Claim 6 to trim the set of potential values of t that need to be tested for this larger value of σ. In greater detail, our algorithm is 1) Let σ cur denote the value of σ that is currently being evaluated as a potential witness. σ cur is initialized to δ max (τ ).
We will also use a variable t cur , initialized to zero.
div.formula: 2) If σ cur is larger than m-U (τ ) m-1 -
div.p: where is an arbitrarily small positive constant that has been a priori determined, then we exit the test, having failed to show τ is EDF-schedulable. Otherwise by the results of Section IV-A, we need only evaluate Condition 1 for values of t ∈ T S(τ, σ cur ) to determine whether it is satisfiable or not. We begin at the smallest value in T S(τ, σ cur ) that is greater than t cur , and consider the values in T S(τ, σ cur ) in increasing order. If no value of t in T S(τ, σ cur ) causes Condition 1 to evaluate to false for this current value of σ cur , then we exit the test, having succeeded in showing that τ is EDFschedulable.

3) Suppose, however, that there is some value of t that causes Condition 1 to evaluate to false for this value of σ cur . Assign t cur this value of t. By Claim 6, if τ is not EDF-schedulable then for all values of σ > σ cur there is some t ≥ t cur which causes Condition 1 to evaluate to false. Let σ new denote the smallest value of σ > σ cur , such that

div.p: Let us examine how work(τ i , t cur , σ) changes as σ is increased in the neighborhood of σ cur , while the task τ i and the interval-length t cur are kept unchanged. As we have previously observed (see also Figure 5 for an example) work(τ i , t, σ) is a piecewise linear function in t comprised of at most |V i | linear segments over the time interval [(k -1)T i , kT i ] for each positive integer k. We can therefore write a linear equation that expresses how work(τ i , t cur , σ) varies as σ is increased from its value σ cur , under the assumption that we remain in the "linear neighborhood" of its current value (i.e., while the linear segment within which t cur falls has not changed). Summing over all tasks τ i yields a linear equation that we can solve to determine a value of σ for which Inequality 7 holds. If this value of σ results in t cur remaining in the same linear segment of the work function work(τ i , t, σ ) as it did in work(τ i , t, σ) for all τ i , we have the desired value for σ new . Otherwise, t cur falls in a different linear segment of the work function work(τ i , t, σ ) than it did in work(τ i , t, σ), which means that our assumption that we have remained in the linear neighborhood of σ cur is false. We must then re-construct the linear equation using a different slope (and offset) for those τ i for which t cur falls in a different linear segment., and re-solve the linear equation to yield a different value of σ . The crucial observation is that since each work function work(τ i , t, σ) is comprised of at most |V i | linear segments over the time interval [(k -1)T i , kT i ] for each positive integer k, we will need to do such re-computation at most i:τi∈τ |V i | times, which is polynomial in the representation of the task system τ .

div.head: E. Properties
div.p: In this section, we establish that our GEDF schedulability test (i) can be implemented efficiently, to have run-time that is pseudo-polynomial in the representation of the task system subject to analysis; and (ii) is superior to the test in [5].

Computational complexity. Observe that the values assigned to the variable t cur during the above algorithm are monotonically increasing. Hence, the total number of times that distinct values get assigned to t cur is no more than the largest cardinality of T S(τ, σ), from among all the values of σ that get tested. And we have seen in Section IV-A that for each value of σ, |T S(τ, σ)| is pseudo-polynomially bounded in the representation of the task system τ . We saw in Section IV-D that σ new can be computed in polynomial time, while the rest of the processing above for a given value of t cur is easily seen to also take polynomial time. This yields the following result: Theorem 3. This EDF-schedulability test has pseudopolynomial time complexity.
The following theorem asserts the dominance of our GEDF schedulability test over the test in [5].

Theorem 4. Any sporadic DAG task system that is determined to be GEDF-schedulable on an m-processor platform by the pseudo-polynomial test in [5] is also determined to be GEDFschedulable on an m-processor platform by the test derived in this section. The converse of this statement is not true: there are task systems determined to be GEDF-schedulable on an m-processor platform by our test, for which the test of [5] fails to establish GEDF-schedulability.

Proof: As shown above, our test exhaustively considers every value σ, δ max (τ ) ≤ σ ≤ 1, as a potential witness to the GEDF-schedulability of task system τ . Hence if m/(2m -1) -the only σ that is tested as a potential witness by the test in [5] -turns out to be a witness to the GEDF-schedulability of τ , this fact will be determined by our test as well.

It is not difficult to construct task systems that the test of [5] fails to identify as being GEDF-schedulable, but our test does. (A trivial such task system would consist of a single task with density > m/(2m -1), whose DAG is a single node with WCET less than the task's deadline, and a period equal to infinity, being schedule don an m-processor system for any m > 1. The test of [5] will not, by definition, find any task system with δ max > m/(2m -1) to be GEDF-schedulable, while it may be verified that our test will discover that setting σ equal to the density of the task results in Condition 1 evaluating to true.)

div.head: V. EXPERIMENTS
div.p: We have conducted some schedulability experiments in an attempt to compare the performance of our GEDFschedulability analysis algorithm with the one in [5] upon randomly-generated systems of sporadic DAG tasks. Although we caution against reading too much into the results of these experiments since these results are necessarily deeply influenced by the manner in which we generate our task systems, the results do indicate that (as expected) our algorithm's performance is generally overwhelmingly superior to that of the one in [5].

We took a "short cut" in implementing the test derived in this paper, in that we made the following pessimistic approximation. If the current value σ cur that we are considering as a potential witness to the GEDF-schedulability is deemed to not be a witness, we increment σ cur by a small constant (0.025) instead of using the technique described in Section IV-D to determine a new candidate witness. This approximation can only disadvantage our technique (since it opens up the possibility that we may have skipped over a viable witness); hence, the conclusions that we draw regarding the effectiveness of our technique over the other ones is not weakened as a consequence of this approximation. We considered this short cut a reasonable approximation in our evaluation experiments, because the technique described in Section IV-D for assigning a value to σ new , the next value of σ to consider as a potential witness, is computationally quite expensive (although it remains in pseudo-polynomial time, as shown in Section IV-D) as well as being quite complex to program. Our schedulability experiments, described below, seem to indicate that even this approximated test performs quite a bit better than earlier tests.

Workload generation. Our random generator for systems of sporadic DAG tasks is based upon the one described in [7]. The generation of each individual task is governed by the following parameters 1) n max : The number of nodes is uniformly chosen within a range (1, n max ). 2) [C lo , C hi ]: The WCET for each node is a positive integer, uniformly chosen to be ≥ C lo and ≤ C hi .

3) p: Each edge is added with a probability p, 0 < p < 1; for each edge, its orientation is chosen to ensure acyclicity. 4) [k lo , k hi ]: The deadline for a task τ i is obtained an integer uniformly chosen within the range [k lo ×len i , k hi ×len i ],

As is evident from these plots, the results are pretty much as expected -the new test is significantly superior to the pseudo-polynomial test of [5] for system utilizations exceeding approximately 50% of the platform capacity. (Both tests consistently out-perform the polynomial-time test also of [5], which is only able to determine a few systems schedulable, and that only for very low system utilizations. In essence, this polynomial-time test seems to be of very limited use across all the parameter combinations we examined.)

div.head: VI. CONCLUSIONS
div.p: Recent work [5], [7] has shown that the global EDF (GEDF) scheduling of recurrent task systems represented using the sporadic DAGs model has a speedup bound of (2-1/m) when implemented upon an m-processor platform. In [5], a pseudopolynomial time GEDF schedulability test with speedup bound within a constant approximative factor of this bound is additionally derived. Although this optimality property makes the schedulability condition in [5] very significant from a conceptual perspective, its applicability in the analysis of actual realtime systems is somewhat limited. A very similar situation had occurred earlier in the case of the multiprocessor scheduling of systems of 3-parameter sporadic tasks [6], [9]: techniques were introduced in [4] that helped established a tight speedup bound for the EDF scheduling of such systems, and these techniques were further exploited in [1], [2] to provide an improved schedulability test. Motivated by that earlier experience, we have built upon the theoretical foundations provided by the [5] test, applying techniques very similar to those introduced in [1], [2] to obtain a sufficient GEDF schedulability test for sporadic DAG task systems that is more widely applicable, and exhibits lower pessimism, than the test of [5] while retaining the optimal processor speedup factor. We have proved the strict dominance of our test over the one in [5]; we have additionally illustrated, via schedulability experiments, the reduced pessimism of this new test. Although the validity of conclusions drawn on the basis of these experiments are limited to task systems with characteristics similar to those generated by our task-generation model, they do serve the purpose of showing that there are at least some classes of systems in which our test significantly out-performs the one in [5]. We have shown that our improved schedulability test can be implemented to have a run-time that is pseudo-polynomial in the representation of the task system being analyzed. Since many algorithms that are currently used in the analysis of real-time systems are of similar computational complexity, this suggests that our schedulability test is efficient enough to be of use in the design and analysis of actual multiprocessor real-time application systems.

Our method of assigning deadlines and periods differs from the one in[7]: their period-assignment formula was designed to ensure that "for small m, tasks tend to have smaller utilization. This allows [...] to have a reasonable number of tasks in a task set for any value of m, Task sets are created by adding tasks to them until the total utilization reaches 99% of m." In contrast, we do not only desire systems with 99% utilization; rather, we have a target utilization that we seek to achieve by repeatedly adding tasks.
